clue.text: Sailed with the shoreline?

parts.note: the clue pictures a boat travelling along beside the land's edge, which also suggests moving without effort

explanation.surface: A sailor asks whether a voyage followed the line of the land.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb also means moved along without effort, as a sailing boat can do hugging the land.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel along beside the land's edge by boat is the original nautical sense of this verb.

clue.text: Smashes right into jars left out

indicators.note: into tells us the letter for right goes inside what remains
out tells us the letter for left is dropped from the word for jars

parts.note: jars as a verb means clashes, grates against

explanation.surface: Someone lashes out at pottery, breaking it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left out' drops L from CLASHES, giving CASHES; 'into' puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Crashes and smashes are both nouns for violent collisions or breakages.

clue.text: Scots place split ends in hair drier

indicators.note: split ends are frayed hair tips; here the outer letters of the phrase are cut off, leaving the town inside

explanation.surface: A hairdressing complaint: the dryer is causing split ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split ends in' looks like a hairdressing worry but signals the run tucked inside the phrase, once its first and last letters go.
explanation.definitionFit: Airdrie is a town in North Lanarkshire, east of Glasgow in Scotland.

clue.text: The most insipid, interminable relations

indicators.note: interminable here means having no ends, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: insipid food is stale, so the most insipid is the stalest

explanation.surface: Someone complains about their dullest, never-ending family members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interminable' strips the first and last letters, S and T, from STALEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A relation can be an account or narrative, so relations are stories.

clue.text: How strange cook appears before he moves in time

indicators.note: appears before places the word for cook ahead of the rearranged letters

parts.note: to cook the books is to doctor them, i.e. falsify

indicators.note: strange tells us the letters of how are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on an odd chef who shows up and then shifts about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' is a verb sense, to falsify, as in cooking the books. 'Strange' rearranges the letters of 'How'; 'appears before' sets the cook word ahead of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the long-running BBC science-fiction series is a Time Lord who travels through time.

clue.text: Glosses over, essentially without copy writers

annotationWithheld.why: Glosses over, essentially without copy writers (7): SCRIBES is plainly copy writers with CRIB (copy) inside S...ES, but no reading of 'Glosses over, essentially' gives S...ES without a word doing two jobs; likely OCR damage
annotationWithheld.clue: Glosses over, essentially without copy writers

clue.text: Mostly gorged, there's a little left inside pan

indicators.note: inside puts that single letter within the shortened word
mostly means all but the last letter of the word for gorged

parts.note: gorged means sated, filled up with food

indicators.note: a little of the word left is just its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone has eaten nearly everything, leaving a scrap in the cooking pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' cuts SATED to SATE; 'a little' takes L from 'left'; 'inside' puts it in, S-L-ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a play is to criticise it harshly, which is also to slate it.

clue.text: Bread maker's funny normality

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A baker's odd ordinariness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' is slang for money, so its maker is the body that strikes coins.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Mint manufactures the UK's coins, and bread is slang for cash.

clue.text: Aims at getting sick on the smallest bit of boiled rice

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the rearranged letters sit under the first letter
the smallest bit of a word is its first letter
getting sick suggests being upset, so the letters of aims at are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone tries to be ill after eating a scrap of cooked grain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting sick' signals the anagram of 'Aims at'; 'on' sets that under the first letter of 'boiled' in this down entry. 'Boiled' belongs to the wordplay, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Basmati is a fragrant long-grain variety commonly served boiled.

clue.text: Diagnostic tests about pressure, my having been uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifted means the whole assembly is read from the bottom upwards
about means the tests go round the other pieces

parts.note: an MOT is the annual UK roadworthiness test for vehicles, so tests are MOTs
P is the standard abbreviation for pressure in physics

explanation.surface: A doctor runs tests on blood pressure, and the patient's mood is lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: MOT is the yearly British roadworthiness check for cars. 'About' wraps the tests round the other two pieces; 'having been uplifted' reverses the lot, giving MOTPMYS turned upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagnostic, used as a noun, is a sign that helps identify a disease.

clue.text: Synthetic elastic Lycra, I see

indicators.note: elastic means stretchable, suggesting the letters can be pulled into a new shape

parts.note: the letter C sounds like the word see

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a stretchy fabric is man-made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elastic' rearranges LYCRA plus I plus C (the letter that sounds like 'see').
explanation.definitionFit: Acrylic is a man-made fibre or resin, the opposite of a natural material.

clue.text: Plant found in lunatic asylums

indicators.note: lunatic means crazy, so the letters of asylums are rearranged

explanation.surface: A flower growing in old mental hospitals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunatic' rearranges ASYLUMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alyssum is a low flowering herb of the cabbage family, often grown in borders.

clue.text: Report on houses

parts.note: sounds like a survey of buildings, but the houses are the twelve divisions of the zodiac in astrology

explanation.surface: An estate agent's survey of properties.
explanation.walkthrough: Astrologers divide the heavens into twelve houses; a reading of them is an astrological forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrological forecast interprets the positions of planets in the twelve houses of the zodiac.

clue.text: Minimum score ultimately seen in final

indicators.note: seen in places that letter inside the word for final

parts.note: final means last

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of score

explanation.surface: The lowest score turned up in the final match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' takes E from 'score'; 'seen in' puts it inside LAST.
explanation.definitionFit: The least is the smallest amount possible, the lowest quantity.

clue.text: Appropriate confirmation. about time

indicators.note: about means the word for confirmation goes round the letter for time

parts.note: a seal on a document confirms it, as in a seal of approval

explanation.surface: Someone says it is fitting that confirmation has come at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' is a verb here, to take for oneself, not the adjective 'suitable'.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate something is to take it without permission, i.e. to pinch it.

clue.text: Quickly desire a whisky?

parts.note: to like something is to want or fancy it
a shot is a single measure of spirits such as whisky

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you fancy a whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an offer of a drink; 'desire' is the verb to fancy, and a shot is a measure of spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means without hesitation, very fast, like a bullet from a gun.

clue.text: Sally's not quite with topless victims in trouble

indicators.note: not quite means the word with loses its last letter
in trouble suggests disorder, so the remaining letters are rearranged
topless means the word victims loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Sally's story about half-dressed victims in a scrape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' cuts WITH to WIT; 'topless' cuts VICTIMS to ICTIMS, which 'in trouble' rearranges as TICISM. 'Sally' is a witty remark, not a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a quick, clever remark, a flash of wit.

clue.text: Boxed 'set Eve and I'd left out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are disordered or wrong, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Eve and I left the TV set off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges SET, EVE, ID and L; 'boxed' means shown on the box, slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: The box is slang for television, so something boxed has been broadcast on TV.

clue.text: Mere raven lands before example of tower

indicators.note: lands before puts the word for raven ahead of the word for mere

parts.note: raven as an adjective means glossy black, as in raven hair
a mere is a lake or pool

explanation.surface: A raven alights beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mere' is a noun, a lake, not 'only'. The seaside town in Lancashire, England, has a famous tower modelled on the Eiffel Tower.
explanation.definitionFit: This resort is famed for its 1894 landmark tower, so it is a place that has one.

clue.text: Portable container for washers

parts.note: sounds like a box for small metal rings, but the washers are people having a bath

explanation.surface: A carry-case for small plumbing parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washers' are people washing themselves, not the rings used with nuts and bolts; an old free-standing bath could be moved about.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-standing bath can be carried and holds people who wash in it.

clue.text: Calm down, silly sausage!

indicators.note: silly suggests foolishness, so the letters of sausage are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend, fondly called a silly sausage, to relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' rearranges SAUSAGE; 'silly sausage' is an affectionate British phrase for a foolish person.
explanation.definitionFit: To assuage is to soothe or ease a feeling such as anger or pain.

clue.text: The balls so regularly dismissed — several ducks resulting?

indicators.note: regularly dismissed means every other letter is thrown out, keeping the alternate ones

explanation.surface: Batsmen are out so often that the team ends up with several ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a batsman's score of zero; here ducks are birds. Take the first, third, fifth letters and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Teal are small freshwater dabbling ducks, so several are a group of them.

clue.text: Adult on, for example, London dock

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the letter for adult sits on top

parts.note: A is the film classification for adult
London Bridge is an example of a crossing over a river

explanation.surface: A grown-up arrives at a London quayside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' is a verb, to cut short, not a quay.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock something is to shorten it, as a text is cut down in an edited version.

clue.text: Prior to confusion, spotted tiniest bits of ash?

indicators.note: prior to places the word for spotted before the word for confusion

parts.note: spotted means saw, caught sight of
dust can mean a commotion or disturbance, as in kicking up a dust

explanation.surface: Before the chaos, someone noticed fine particles of ash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ash' is the tree, so its smallest bits are wood shavings from a saw, not cinders.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawing timber such as ash produces fine particles of wood.

clue.text: Curiously, least attractive unit

indicators.note: curiously means oddly, so the letters of least are rearranged

explanation.surface: Strangely, the least appealing part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attractive' means magnetic: the SI unit of magnetic flux density.
explanation.definitionFit: The SI unit of magnetic flux density is named after the inventor Nikola Tesla.

clue.text: Take vowels a out 'out; it would suit you

indicators.note: out suggests disorder, so the gathered letters are rearranged

parts.note: R, from Latin recipe, is the abbreviation for take on prescriptions

explanation.surface: An instruction to strip certain vowels from a word.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints an apostrophe where the letter I belongs. 'Out' rearranges R, VOWELS, A and I; the London street is famous for tailors.
explanation.definitionFit: This London street is home to bespoke tailors who make made-to-measure clothing.

clue.text: Old vessel at sea backing a bit

indicators.note: in a down clue, backing means that portion is read in reverse
a bit means a portion of the letters of vessel at sea is taken

explanation.surface: An old ship at sea sails backwards a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit' takes ELATS from 'vessEL AT Sea'; 'backing' turns it around.
explanation.definitionFit: Stale means no longer fresh, as food or news that has grown old.

clue.text: Channels energy into dissolving salt

indicators.note: into places the letter for energy inside those rearranged letters
dissolving suggests breaking up, so the letters of salt are rearranged

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Energy is put into dissolving salt, as in a chemistry experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dissolving' rearranges SALT to LATS; 'into' puts E inside after the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Leats are open watercourses that carry water to a mill wheel.

clue.text: Mostly catch pain inside windpipe

indicators.note: inside places the word for pain within what remains
mostly means the word for catch loses its final letter

parts.note: to catch an animal is to trap it
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: Someone nearly catches a pain in the throat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' signals one letter dropped from the word for catch, and 'catch' is that word, not the definition; 'inside' puts the pain word within it.
explanation.definitionFit: The trachea is the anatomical name for the airway from larynx to lungs.

clue.text: Odds and evens in Kabul prison

parts.note: SP is starting price in horse racing, the odds at the off
taken as written

indicators.note: evens in means the even-numbered letters of Kabul, the second and fourth

explanation.surface: A bookmaker sets odds and evens in Afghanistan's capital jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odds and evens' looks like one phrase but splits into three pieces; 'evens in' picks the 2nd and 4th letters of Kabul. Spandau was the Berlin jail that held Nazi war criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: Spandau Prison in Berlin held Nazi war criminals after the Nuremberg trials.

clue.text: Infuse brew of herb tea

indicators.note: a brew is a mixture, so the letters of herb tea are stirred together anew

explanation.surface: Steep a pot of herbal tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brew of' rearranges HERBTEA; 'infuse' here means instil, as to breathe life into something.
explanation.definitionFit: To infuse is to instil, as to breathe new life or spirit into something.

clue.text: Dismember a girl's body

parts.note: Di is a short form of the girl's name Diana, with the possessive s
a sect is a body of followers

explanation.surface: A grim instruction to cut up a woman's corpse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' is a group of people, not a corpse; DI'S plus SECT.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissect is to cut apart, as an anatomist takes a specimen to pieces.
